segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we had been brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The natives showed us no ordinary kindness: they lit a fire and welcomed us all, because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man must certainly be a murderer. Though he was brought safely out of the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after they had waited a long time and saw nothing out of the ordinary happening to him, they changed their minds and began to say he was a god.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the area around that place there were estates belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It happened that Publius’s father was lying ill, suffering from bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses also kept coming and were cured.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They also honored us with many honors, and when we were putting out to sea they put on board what we needed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered at the island, an Alexandrian ship with the Dioscuri as its emblem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there we weighed anchor and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The brothers from there, having heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we entered Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, I have done nothing against the people or our ancestral customs, yet I was handed over from Jerusalem as a prisoner into the hands of the Romans,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: who, after examining me, wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But when the Jews spoke against this, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, though not because I had any charge to bring against my nation.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason, then, I asked to see you and speak with you, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I wear this chain.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers who came here reported or said anything bad about you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we would like to hear from you what your views are, for as regards this sect, we know that it is spoken against everywhere.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They set a day with him and came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning until evening he laid the matter out for them, bearing solemn witness to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some were persuaded by what was said, but others refused to believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Disagreeing among themselves, they began to leave after Paul had said one thing:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your ancestors,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: saying, ‘Go to this people and say: You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have become hard of hearing, and their eyes they have shut; otherwise they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will indeed hear.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stayed two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness, unhindered.

notes.note: The Greek word described anyone who did not speak Greek and carried no necessary suggestion of savagery; the Maltese of this period largely spoke a Punic dialect. "Barbarians" now implies brutality, which the verse itself contradicts by praising their kindness. Most modern translations likewise use "natives" or "islanders".

The islanders speak of justice as a personal power that pursues the guilty. Greek tradition personified it as the goddess Dike, and the speakers may have in mind her or a local equivalent. Older versions render it "vengeance"; most modern ones capitalize "Justice".

notes.phrase: the leading man of the island
notes.traditional: the chief man of the island
notes.note: Literally "the first man of the island." This appears to be a recognized local title, not just a description, and inscriptions from Malta are usually cited as attesting it. Whether Publius was the senior Roman official or the foremost local benefactor is not certain.

notes.traditional: Castor and Pollux / the Twin Brothers
notes.note: The Dioscuri ("sons of Zeus") were the twin gods Castor and Pollux, widely regarded as protectors of sailors. Ships carried a carved or painted emblem at the bow that served as their name, so this ship was in effect called "The Dioscuri."

notes.traditional: fetched a compass / made a circuit / set sail
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between a word meaning "taking away" (understood as casting off or raising the anchors, as in 27:40) and a very similar word meaning "going around," which would describe a tacking or circuitous course. The edition translated here adopts the first. The sense of either reading in this nautical context is somewhat uncertain.

notes.phrase: the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns
notes.traditional: Appii Forum and The Three Taverns
notes.note: These were two stopping places on the Appian Way, the main road south from Rome, roughly forty and thirty miles from the city. Believers from Rome travelled a day or more on foot to escort Paul in, a courtesy normally shown to an arriving dignitary.

The Greek word here is the same one translated "Gentiles" in verse 28. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Israel; in the plural it commonly means the non-Jewish peoples. English has no single word that covers both uses.

notes.traditional: Hearing you will hear / You will indeed hear
notes.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 in the wording of the Greek Septuagint. The doubled expressions ("with hearing you will hear," "looking you will look") reproduce a Hebrew idiom of emphasis. The same passage is quoted in the Gospels to explain why many did not respond to Jesus.

Verse 29 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek edition translated here. Later manuscripts add: "And when he had said these things, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves." Most scholars regard it as a later addition to smooth the transition.

Elsewhere the Greek noun means a price or rent paid, which gives "at his own expense." Many translations render it "in his own rented house," which fits the verb "stayed" naturally but is a sense not clearly attested for this word outside this verse. Either way, Paul was paying for private lodging while under guard.

candidates.reason: It recurs in Romans 1:14, 1 Corinthians 14:11 and Colossians 3:11, where "barbarian", "foreigner", "non-Greek" and "native" are all plausible and the traditional word misleads.
The plural covers fellow believers of both sexes and also fellow Jews (v. 21), so the choice between "brothers", "brothers and sisters" and "believers" needs one policy across the New Testament.
It is used in Acts of the Sadducees, Pharisees and Christians and in the letters of factions, so translators vary between "sect", "party", "faction" and "heresy".
It is frequent in John, Acts, Paul, Hebrews and 1 John with renderings ranging over "boldness", "openness", "confidence" and "plainly", and needs a decision by sense.
"Kingdom of God" is pervasive, and whether to render it "kingdom", "reign" or "rule" should be decided once for the whole New Testament.
